title: Chapter 16 — The Ship
paragraphs: That night in bed, we worked out our plans for the next day. But to my surprise and no small concern, Queequeg now gave me to understand that he had been diligently consulting Yojo — the name of his little black god — and Yojo had told him two or three times over, and strongly insisted on it in every way, that instead of the two of us going together among the whaling fleet in the harbor and choosing our ship jointly — instead of this, I say, Yojo earnestly directed that the choice of the ship should rest entirely with me, since Yojo meant to befriend us. To that end he had already picked out a vessel which I, Ishmael, left to myself, would be certain to hit upon, exactly as though it had happened by chance. And I was to sign on to that vessel immediately, leaving Queequeg out of it for the present.

I have forgotten to mention that, in many things, Queequeg placed great trust in the excellence of Yojo's judgment and his surprising foresight. He regarded Yojo with considerable esteem, as a fairly decent sort of god who perhaps meant well enough on the whole, but who did not, in all cases, succeed in his well-meaning plans.

Now, this plan of Queequeg's — or rather Yojo's — about choosing our ship: I didn't like that plan at all. I had counted a good deal on Queequeg's shrewdness to point out the whaler best fitted to carry us and our fortunes safely. But since all my objections had no effect on Queequeg, I had to give in; and so I got ready to go at the business with a determined, rushing sort of energy and vigor that would quickly settle that trifling little affair. Early the next morning, I left Queequeg shut up with Yojo in our little bedroom — for it seemed that for Queequeg and Yojo that day was some sort of Lent or Ramadan, a day of fasting, humiliation, and prayer. How it worked I never could find out, because though I applied myself to it several times, I never could master his liturgies and his Thirty-Nine Articles. Leaving Queequeg, then, fasting over his tomahawk pipe, and Yojo warming himself at his sacrificial fire of wood shavings, I set out among the shipping. After a long stretch of wandering and many random inquiries, I learned that there were three ships taking on crews for three-year voyages — the Devil-dam, the Tit-bit, and the Pequod. Devil-Dam, I don't know the origin of; Tit-bit is obvious; Pequod, you will no doubt remember, was the name of a celebrated tribe of Massachusetts Indians, now as extinct as the ancient Medes. I peered and pried around the Devil-dam; from her I hopped over to the Tit-bit; and finally, going aboard the Pequod and looking around her for a moment, I decided that this was the very ship for us.

You may have seen many a quaint craft in your day, for all I know — square-toed luggers, mountainous Japanese junks, butter-box galliots, and whatnot. But take my word for it, you never saw such a rare old craft as this same rare old Pequod. She was a ship of the old school, rather small if anything, with an old-fashioned, claw-footed look about her. Long seasoned and weather-stained in the typhoons and calms of all four oceans, her old hull's complexion was darkened like that of a French grenadier who has fought in both Egypt and Siberia. Her venerable bows looked bearded. Her masts — cut somewhere on the coast of Japan, where her original ones were lost overboard in a gale — her masts stood stiffly up like the spines of the three old kings of Cologne. Her ancient decks were worn and wrinkled, like the pilgrim-worshipped flagstone in Canterbury Cathedral where Becket bled. But to all these old antiquities of hers were added new and marvelous features, belonging to the wild business she had followed for more than half a century. Old Captain Peleg, for many years her chief mate before he commanded a vessel of his own, and now a retired seaman and one of the principal owners of the Pequod — this old Peleg, during his time as chief mate, had built upon her original grotesqueness and inlaid it all over with a quaintness of both material and design unmatched by anything, unless it be Thorkill-Hake's carved buckler or bedstead. She was decked out like some barbaric Ethiopian emperor, his neck heavy with pendants of polished ivory. She was a thing of trophies. A cannibal of a craft, dressing herself up in the carved bones of her enemies. All around, her unpaneled, open bulwarks were garnished like one continuous jaw with the long, sharp teeth of the sperm whale, set there as pins to fasten her old hempen sinews and tendons to. Those sinews did not run through lowly blocks of land wood but traveled deftly over sheaves of sea-ivory. Scorning a turnstile wheel at her reverend helm, she sported a tiller there; and that tiller was in one piece, curiously carved from the long, narrow lower jaw of her hereditary foe. The helmsman who steered by that tiller in a storm felt like the Tartar holding back his fiery steed by clutching its jaw. A noble craft, but somehow a most melancholy one! All noble things are touched with that.

When I looked around the quarter-deck for someone in authority, so as to offer myself as a candidate for the voyage, at first I saw nobody. But I couldn't very well overlook a strange sort of tent, or rather wigwam, pitched a little behind the mainmast. It seemed to be only a temporary structure used in port. It was cone-shaped, some ten feet high, made of the long, huge slabs of flexible black bone taken from the middle and highest part of the right whale's jaws. A circle of these slabs, planted with their broad ends on the deck and laced together, sloped in toward one another and joined at the top in a tufted point, where the loose, hairy fibers waved back and forth like the topknot on the head of some old Pottowottamie Sachem, or chief. A triangular opening faced the bow of the ship, so that whoever sat inside had a complete view forward.

Half hidden in this strange shelter, I finally found someone who looked like he had authority. It was noon, the ship's work was paused, and he was enjoying a break from the burden of command. He sat in an old-fashioned oak chair, wriggling all over with curious carving, its seat formed of a stout interlacing of the same springy material as the wigwam.

There was nothing so very remarkable, perhaps, about the appearance of the elderly man I saw. He was brown and muscular, like most old seamen, and heavily bundled in blue pilot-cloth cut in the Quaker style. The only notable thing was a fine, almost microscopic network of the tiniest wrinkles around his eyes, which must have come from years of sailing through hard gales and always squinting into the wind — that habit tightens the muscles around the eyes. Wrinkles like that are very effective in a scowl.
"Is this the Captain of the Pequod?" I said, stepping up to the entrance of the tent.
"Supposing it is the captain of the Pequod, what do you want with him?" he demanded.
"I was thinking of signing on."
"Were you now? I can see you're no Nantucketer. Ever been in a stove boat?"
"No, Sir, I never have."
"Don't know anything at all about whaling, I suppose — eh?"
"Nothing, Sir, but I have no doubt I'll learn quickly. I've made several voyages in the merchant service, and I think that —"

"Merchant service be damned. Don't talk that lingo to me. See that leg? I'll take that leg off your stern if you ever talk of the marchant service to me again. Marchant service indeed! I suppose now you feel considerable proud of having served in those marchant ships. But flukes! Man, what makes you want to go whaling, eh? It looks a little suspicious, doesn't it, eh? You haven't been a pirate, have you? Didn't rob your last captain, did you? Not thinking of murdering the officers once you get to sea?"

I protested my innocence. I could see that behind the mask of these half-humorous insinuations, this old seaman, as an insulated, Quakerish Nantucketer, was full of his insular prejudices. He was rather suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.
"But what draws you to whaling? I want to know that before I think about signing you on."
"Well, sir, I want to see what whaling is. I want to see the world."
"Want to see what whaling is, eh? Have you set eyes on Captain Ahab?"
"Who is Captain Ahab, sir?"
"That's what I thought. Captain Ahab is the captain of this ship."
"I'm mistaken then. I thought I was speaking to the captain himself."

"You're speaking to Captain Peleg — that's who you're speaking to, young man. It's my job, mine and Captain Bildad's, to see the Pequod fitted out for the voyage and supplied with everything she needs, including crew. We're part owners and agents. But as I was saying, if you want to know what whaling is, as you say you do, I can show you a way to find out before you commit yourself past backing out. Take a look at Captain Ahab, young man, and you'll find he has only one leg."
"What do you mean, sir? Was the other one lost by a whale?"
"Lost by a whale! Young man, come closer to me: it was devoured, chewed up, crunched by the most monstrous parmacetty that ever chipped a boat! — ah, ah!"

I was a little alarmed by his intensity, and perhaps also a little moved by the genuine grief in that final exclamation. But I said as calmly as I could, "What you say is no doubt true enough, sir. But how could I have known there was anything especially ferocious about that particular whale, though I might have guessed as much from the simple fact of the accident?"
"Look here, young man, your lungs are sort of soft, do you see; you don't talk shark a bit. Sure you've been to sea before now? Sure of that?"
"Sir," said I, "I thought I told you that I'd been on four voyages in the merchant —"

"Hard down out of that! Mind what I said about the marchant service — don't aggravate me — I won't have it. But let's understand each other. I've given you a hint about what whaling is; do you still feel inclined for it?"
"I do, sir."
"Very good. Now, are you the kind of man who'd throw a harpoon down a live whale's throat and then jump in after it? Answer quick!"
"I am, sir, if it were absolutely necessary and there were no alternative — which I don't believe is actually the case."

"Good again. So you not only want to go whaling to find out what it's like, but you also want to see the world? Wasn't that what you said? I thought so. Well then, just step forward there and take a look over the weather bow. Then come back and tell me what you see."

For a moment I stood puzzled by this odd request, not sure whether to take it as a joke or seriously. But when Captain Peleg concentrated all his crow's feet into one fierce scowl, he sent me on my way.

Walking forward and looking over the weather bow, I saw that the ship, swinging on her anchor with the rising tide, was now pointing at a slant toward the open ocean. The view was unlimited but utterly monotonous and forbidding. Not the slightest variety that I could see.
"Well, what's the report?" said Peleg when I came back. "What did you see?"
"Not much," I replied. "Nothing but water. Plenty of horizon, though, and there's a squall coming up, I think."
"Well, what do you think now about seeing the world? Still want to go around Cape Horn to see more of it, eh? Can't you see the world right where you stand?"

I was a little taken aback, but go whaling I must and would. The Pequod was as good a ship as any — I thought the best — and I repeated all this to Peleg. Seeing how determined I was, he agreed to sign me on.
"You might as well sign the papers right now," he added. "Come along." And with that, he led the way below deck into the cabin.

Sitting on the stern bench was what struck me as a most unusual and surprising figure. This turned out to be Captain Bildad, who along with Captain Peleg was one of the largest owners of the vessel. The remaining shares, as is sometimes the case in these ports, were held by a crowd of old pensioners — widows, orphaned children, and wards of the court — each owning about the value of a timber head, a foot of plank, or a nail or two in the ship. People in Nantucket invest their money in whaling vessels the same way that you invest yours in approved state stocks that bring in good interest.

Now, Bildad, like Peleg and indeed many Nantucketers, was a Quaker. The island had originally been settled by that sect, and to this day its inhabitants generally retain Quaker peculiarities to an unusual degree, though strangely modified by completely foreign influences. Some of these Quakers are the most bloodthirsty of all sailors and whale hunters. They are fighting Quakers — Quakers with a vengeance.

So there are cases among them of men who were given Scripture names — a remarkably common fashion on the island — and who in childhood naturally absorbed the stately, dramatic "thee" and "thou" of the Quaker idiom; yet, from the audacious, daring, and boundless adventure of their later lives, they strangely blend with these peculiarities they never outgrew a thousand bold dashes of character not unworthy of a Scandinavian sea-king or a poetical pagan Roman. And when these things unite in a man of greatly superior natural force, with a globular brain and a ponderous heart; who has also, through the stillness and seclusion of many long night watches in the remotest waters, beneath constellations never seen here in the north, been led to think untraditionally and independently; receiving all nature's sweet or savage impressions fresh from her own virgin, voluntary, and confiding breast, and thereby chiefly, though with some help from accidental advantages, learning a bold, sinewy, lofty language — that man makes one in a whole nation's census: a mighty pageant creature, formed for noble tragedies. Nor will it detract from him at all, seen dramatically, if either by birth or by other circumstances he has what seems a half-willful, overruling morbidness at the bottom of his nature. For all men who are tragically great are made so through a certain morbidness. Be sure of this, O young ambition: all mortal greatness is only disease. But we are not yet dealing with such a man — rather with quite another; and still a man whose peculiarity, if he is indeed peculiar, again results only from another phase of the Quaker, modified by individual circumstances.

Like Captain Peleg, Captain Bildad was a well-to-do, retired whaleman. But unlike Captain Peleg — who didn't care a straw for what are called serious things, and in fact considered those very same serious things the most trifling of all trifles — Captain Bildad had not only been raised from the first in the strictest sect of Nantucket Quakerism, but all his later life at sea, and the sight of many unclothed, lovely island creatures round the Horn — all that had not moved this native-born Quaker one single jot, had not so much as altered one angle of his vest. Still, for all this unchangeableness, there was some lack of plain consistency about worthy Captain Bildad. Though he refused, from conscientious scruples, to bear arms against invaders on land, he had himself boundlessly invaded the Atlantic and the Pacific; and though a sworn enemy of human bloodshed, he had, in his straight-bodied coat, spilled tuns upon tuns of leviathan gore. How the pious Bildad, now in the contemplative evening of his days, reconciled these things in memory, I don't know. But it didn't seem to concern him much, and very probably he had long since come to the wise and sensible conclusion that a man's religion is one thing and this practical world quite another. This world pays dividends. Rising from a little cabin boy in short clothes of the drabbest drab to a harpooner in a broad shad-bellied waistcoat; from that to boat-header, chief mate, and captain, and finally ship owner — Bildad, as I hinted before, had concluded his adventurous career by retiring wholly from active life at the goodly age of sixty and devoting his remaining days to the quiet receiving of his well-earned income.

Now, Bildad, I'm sorry to say, had the reputation of being a hopeless old miser, and in his sea-going days, a bitter, hard taskmaster. They told me in Nantucket, though it certainly seems a curious story, that when he sailed the old Categut whaler, his crew, upon arriving home, were mostly all carried ashore to the hospital, utterly exhausted and worn out. For a pious man, especially a Quaker, he was certainly rather hard-hearted, to say the least. He never swore at his men, they said. But somehow he got an enormous amount of cruel, unrelenting hard work out of them. When Bildad was chief mate, having his drab-colored eye fixed intently on you made you feel completely nervous until you could grab something — a hammer or a marlinspike — and go to work like a madman at something or other, never mind what. Laziness and idleness withered before him. His own body was the perfect expression of his utilitarian character. On his long, gaunt frame, he carried no spare flesh and no unnecessary beard — just a soft, economical fuzz on his chin, like the worn nap of his broad-brimmed hat.

Such was the person I saw sitting on the stern bench when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small. There, bolt upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat that way and never leaned — this to preserve his coat tails. His broad-brimmed hat was placed beside him. His legs were stiffly crossed. His drab clothes were buttoned up to his chin. And with spectacles on his nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a heavy volume.
"Bildad," cried Captain Peleg, "at it again, Bildad, eh? You've been studying those Scriptures now for the last thirty years, to my certain knowledge. How far have you got, Bildad?"
As if long accustomed to such irreverent talk from his old shipmate, Bildad paid no attention to the disrespect. He quietly looked up, saw me, and glanced inquiringly at Peleg.
"He says he's our man, Bildad," said Peleg. "He wants to sign on."
"Does thee?" said Bildad, in a hollow tone, turning to face me.
"I does," I said, unconsciously mimicking him — he was that intense a Quaker.
"What do you think of him, Bildad?" said Peleg.
"He'll do," said Bildad, looking me over. Then he went on spelling his way through his book in a mumbling tone, quite audible.

I thought him the strangest old Quaker I'd ever seen, especially since Peleg, his friend and old shipmate, seemed like such a blowhard. But I said nothing, only looking around me sharply. Peleg threw open a chest, pulled out the ship's articles, set pen and ink before him, and sat down at a small table. I began to think it was time to figure out what terms I'd accept for the voyage. I already knew that in the whaling business they paid no wages. Instead, everyone, including the captain, received shares of the profits called lays. These lays were proportional to the importance of each man's duties. I also knew that as a green hand at whaling, my own lay wouldn't be large. But considering that I was used to the sea, could steer a ship, splice a rope, and all that, I had no doubt, from everything I had heard, that I would be offered at least the 275th lay — that is, the 275th part of the clear net proceeds of the voyage, whatever that might amount to. And though the 275th lay was what they called a rather long lay, it was better than nothing. If we had a lucky voyage, it might nearly cover the cost of the clothes I'd wear out, to say nothing of three years' food and board, for which I wouldn't have to pay a penny.

You might think this was a poor way to pile up a princely fortune — and so it was, a very poor way indeed. But I'm one of those people who never fuss about princely fortunes, and I'm quite content if the world is ready to feed and house me while I'm putting up at this grim sign of the Thunder Cloud. All things considered, I thought the 275th lay would be about the fair thing, though I wouldn't have been surprised to be offered the 200th, given my broad-shouldered build.

But one thing, nevertheless, made me a little uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other, lesser and scattered owners left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. And for all I knew, stingy old Bildad might have a great deal of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was vainly trying to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"
"Well, Captain Bildad," Peleg interrupted, "what do you say? What lay shall we give this young man?"
"You know best," came the sepulchral reply. "The seven hundred and seventy-seventh wouldn't be too much, would it? — 'where moth and rust do corrupt, but lay —'"

Lay indeed, I thought, and such a lay! The seven hundred and seventy-seventh! Well, old Bildad, you're determined that I, for one, shall not lay up many lays here below, where moth and rust do corrupt. That was an exceedingly long lay indeed. And though the size of the figure might at first deceive a landsman, the slightest thought will show that though seven hundred and seventy-seven is a pretty large number, yet when you come to make a "teenth" of it — a fraction — you will see, I say, that the seven hundred and seventy-seventh part of a farthing is a good deal less than seven hundred and seventy-seven gold doubloons. And so I thought at the time.
"Why, blast your eyes, Bildad," cried Peleg, "you don't want to swindle this young man! He must have more than that."
"Seven hundred and seventy-seventh," Bildad said again, without lifting his eyes. Then he went on mumbling: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also."
"I'm putting him down for the three hundredth," said Peleg. "Do you hear that, Bildad? The three hundredth lay, I say."

Bildad laid down his book and, turning solemnly toward him, said, "Captain Peleg, you have a generous heart. But you must consider the duty you owe to the other owners of this ship — widows and orphans, many of them — and that if we reward the labors of this young man too abundantly, we may be taking the bread from those widows and those orphans. The seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, Captain Peleg."

"You Bildad!" roared Peleg, starting up and clattering about the cabin. "Blast you, Captain Bildad, if I had followed your advice in these matters, I'd have had a conscience by now to lug around that would be heavy enough to founder the largest ship that ever sailed round Cape Horn."

"Captain Peleg," said Bildad steadily, "your conscience may be drawing ten inches of water, or ten fathoms — I can't tell. But since you are still an impenitent man, Captain Peleg, I greatly fear your conscience is only a leaky one, and will in the end sink you, foundering, down to the fiery pit, Captain Peleg."

"Fiery pit! Fiery pit! You insult me, man — past all natural bearing, you insult me. It's an all-fired outrage to tell any human creature that he's bound for hell. Flukes and flames! Bildad, say that again to me, and start my soul-bolts, but I'll — I'll — yes, I'll swallow a live goat with all his hair and horns on. Out of the cabin, you canting, drab-colored son of a wooden gun — a straight wake with you!"
As he thundered this out, he rushed at Bildad. But with a marvelous sideways, sliding quickness, Bildad dodged him that time.

Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal and responsible owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to impenitent Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he twitched a little, as if still nervously agitated. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."
"Captain Peleg," said I, "I have a friend who wants to sign on too — shall I bring him down tomorrow?"
"Of course," said Peleg. "Bring him along and we'll have a look at him."
"What lay does he want?" groaned Bildad, glancing up from the book in which he had again buried himself.
"Oh, never mind about that, Bildad," said Peleg. "Has he ever whaled?" he asked, turning to me.
"Killed more whales than I can count, Captain Peleg."
"Well, bring him along then."
And after signing the papers, off I went, fully confident that I had done a good morning's work and that the Pequod was the very ship Yojo had chosen to carry Queequeg and me around the Cape.

But I hadn't gone far before it struck me that the captain I was to sail with still remained unseen. In many cases, a whale ship will be completely fitted out and take on her entire crew before the captain shows up to take command. Sometimes these voyages last so long, and the time ashore between them is so short, that if the captain has a family or any pressing personal matters, he doesn't bother much with his ship in port but leaves everything to the owners until she's ready for sea. Still, it's always wise to have a look at him before irrevocably putting yourself in his hands. Turning back, I found Captain Peleg and asked where Captain Ahab might be.
"And what do you want with Captain Ahab? Everything's fine — you're signed on."
"Yes, but I'd like to see him."

"I don't think you'll be able to right now. I don't know exactly what's the matter with him, but he stays shut up inside his house. He's a sort of sick, and yet he doesn't look it. Actually, he isn't sick — but he isn't well either. Anyway, young man, he won't always see even me, so I don't suppose he'll see you. He's a strange man, Captain Ahab — so some think — but a good one. Oh, you'll like him well enough, no fear. He's a grand, ungodly, god-like man, Captain Ahab. He doesn't talk much, but when he does, you'd better listen. Be warned: Ahab is above the common run. He's been in colleges as well as among cannibals. He's faced deeper wonders than the waves and driven his fiery lance into mightier, stranger enemies than whales. His lance! The keenest and truest that ever came from all our island! Oh, he's not Captain Bildad, no, and he's not Captain Peleg. He's Ahab, boy. And Ahab of old, as you know, was a crowned king!"
"And a very wicked one. When that evil king was killed, the dogs licked his blood, did they not?"

"Come here — closer, closer," said Peleg, with a look in his eye that nearly startled me. "Listen, lad. Never say that aboard the Pequod. Never say it anywhere. Captain Ahab did not name himself. It was a foolish, ignorant whim of his crazy, widowed mother, who died when he was only a year old. And yet the old squaw Tistig, at Gay Head, said the name would somehow prove prophetic. And perhaps other fools like her may tell you the same. I want to warn you — it's a lie. I know Captain Ahab well. I've sailed with him as mate, years ago. I know what he is — a good man. Not a pious, good man like Bildad, but a swearing good man — something like me — only there's a good deal more of him. I'll admit he was never very cheerful. And I know that on the way home last voyage, he was a little out of his mind for a while. But that was the sharp, shooting pains in his bleeding stump — anyone could see that. I know, too, that ever since he lost his leg on the last voyage to that accursed whale, he's been moody — desperately moody, and savage sometimes. But that will pass. And once and for all, let me tell you and assure you, young man: it's better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one. So goodbye — and don't wrong Captain Ahab just because he happens to have a wicked name. Besides, my boy, he has a wife — married not three voyages ago — a sweet, resigned girl. Think about that. By that sweet girl, the old man has a child. Can you hold, then, that there's any utter, hopeless harm in Ahab? No, no, my lad. Stricken and blasted as he may be, Ahab has his humanities!"

As I walked away, I was full of thoughtfulness. What had been incidentally revealed to me about Captain Ahab filled me with a certain wild, vague painfulness concerning him. And somehow, at the time, I felt a sympathy and a sorrow for him, though for what I don't know, unless it was the cruel loss of his leg. And yet I also felt a strange awe of him; but that sort of awe, which I can't describe at all, was not exactly awe. I don't know what it was. But I felt it, and it didn't turn me against him, though I felt impatient at what seemed like mystery in him, known to me as imperfectly as he was then. Eventually, though, my thoughts were carried off in other directions, so that for the present dark Ahab slipped my mind.
